stem: According to the text, what surprised Vik?
stimulus: Ornithologist Hanne Vik spent three summers tracking Arctic terns that nest on a remote northern island. Most of the birds she tagged were between four and twenty years old, but the oldest, a female first banded as a chick, was 31 when Vik recaptured her. Terns typically begin breeding at about age three, and few are thought to keep breeding past their mid-twenties. The 31-year-old bird, however, was still raising chicks, a fact that surprised Vik even more than the bird's age.
choices: That the oldest tern she recaptured was still raising chicks
That most of the terns she tagged were between four and twenty
That terns typically begin breeding at about three years of age
That a tern first banded as a chick could ever be recaptured
explanation: The last sentence answers the question directly: the 31-year-old bird 'was still raising chicks, a fact that surprised Vik.' Choice A restates that sentence.

B.why: The passage does say this about the age range, but it is background information. Nothing says the range surprised Vik. You chose a true detail that answers a different question.

C.why: This is a general fact about terns that the passage gives as context. The text never says it surprised Vik. You matched words from the passage without checking that they answer 'what surprised.'

D.why: The passage mentions that the bird was banded as a chick and later recaptured, but it never says the recapture itself was surprising. You added a reaction the text does not state.

stem: According to the text, why was Imbert concerned about the school lunches?
stimulus: In a survey of 140 school cafeterias, nutrition scientist Rosa Imbert found that most lunches met federal limits on sodium and saturated fat. Her concern lay elsewhere: fewer than a third of the meals contained enough fiber, a nutrient linked to steady energy and healthy digestion in children. Imbert has proposed that schools replace refined grains with whole-grain versions, a change she estimates would cost districts very little. She also recommends adding beans to at least two lunch menus each week.
choices: Most of the lunches exceeded federal limits on sodium and fat.
Fewer than a third of the lunches contained enough fiber.
Schools could not afford to switch to whole-grain foods.
Beans appeared on fewer than two lunch menus each week.
explanation: The sentence beginning 'Her concern lay elsewhere' answers the question: fewer than a third of the meals had enough fiber. Choice B restates it.

A.why: The passage says most lunches met the sodium and fat limits. You picked up the words 'sodium' and 'fat' and reversed what the text says about them.

C.why: Whole grains come up in Imbert's proposed solution, and she estimates the switch would cost 'very little.' You treated the proposed fix as the cause of her concern and flipped her cost estimate.

D.why: Imbert recommends adding beans to two menus a week, but the passage never says how often beans currently appear. You turned a recommendation into a finding the text does not report.

stem: According to the text, how did Anand's approach differ from that of other researchers?
stimulus: Most studies of how much ride-hailing drivers work have relied on surveys in which drivers estimate their own weekly hours. Labor economist Dev Anand suspected that such estimates ran high. So rather than asking drivers, he analyzed four million trip records supplied by a ride-hailing company. The records showed that drivers worked an average of 19 hours per week, about six fewer than survey respondents in earlier studies had reported.
choices: He analyzed trip records instead of asking drivers for estimates.
He found that drivers worked an average of 19 hours per week.
He surveyed drivers directly about the hours they worked weekly.
He studied drivers who worked six more hours than the average.
explanation: The passage contrasts surveys of drivers with Anand's choice to analyze 'four million trip records' 'rather than asking drivers.' Choice A describes that difference in method.

B.why: This is Anand's result, not his approach. The question asks how his method differed, and you answered with what the method found.

C.why: Surveys are what other researchers used. Anand deliberately avoided them. You gave Anand the approach that belongs to the other researchers.

D.why: The number six is the gap between survey reports and Anand's finding. It does not describe a group of drivers he studied. You took a number from another part of the passage and attached it to the wrong thing.

stem: According to the text, what did officials in Arlen do in response to the 2022 rise in measles cases?
stimulus: In 2022, health officials in the city of Arlen faced a rise in measles cases concentrated in two neighborhoods. During earlier outbreaks, the city had opened a single central clinic. This time, officials sent mobile vaccination vans to schools and markets in the affected areas. Within six weeks, vaccination rates in those neighborhoods rose from 81 percent to 93 percent. Officials credit the vans' convenience, though they note that a radio campaign running at the same time may also have helped.
choices: They opened a single central clinic to serve the entire city.
They sent mobile vaccination vans into the affected areas.
They raised vaccination rates in every neighborhood to 93 percent.
They ran a radio campaign in place of offering vaccinations.
explanation: The sentence beginning 'This time' says officials 'sent mobile vaccination vans to schools and markets in the affected areas.' Choice B restates that sentence.

A.why: The central clinic was the city's response to earlier outbreaks. The 2022 approach was set up as a contrast to it. You took a detail from the wrong time period.

C.why: The 93 percent figure applies only to the two affected neighborhoods. You took a real number from the passage and applied it to every neighborhood in the city.

D.why: The radio campaign ran alongside the vans and did not replace vaccination. You took a secondary detail and made it the main response.

stem: According to the text, what did Marten base his depiction of Lake Sorrel on?
stimulus: For centuries, mapmakers filled unexplored regions with features they had never seen. For example, an 1804 map by cartographer Elias Marten showed a large lake, which he named Lake Sorrel, at the center of an inland plateau. Marten never visited the plateau. Instead, he relied on a trader's secondhand account of the region. Later mapmakers copied the lake onto their own maps for decades. Not until 1871 did a survey team cross the plateau, and it found only dry grassland where the lake was supposed to be.
choices: A trader's secondhand account of the region
His own visit to the center of the plateau
A survey team's crossing of the plateau
Maps drawn by other mapmakers of the time
explanation: The text says Marten 'relied on a trader's secondhand account of the region.' Choice A matches that line.

B.why: The passage states plainly that Marten 'never visited the plateau.' You chose the opposite of what the text says.

C.why: The survey team crossed the plateau in 1871, decades after Marten's map, and showed that the lake did not exist. You used a detail from a later part of the passage that answers a different question.

D.why: In the passage, other mapmakers copied Marten, not the other way around. You reversed the direction of the copying.

stem: According to the text, approximately how long ago did the oldest earthquake Owusu identified occur?
stimulus: Seismologists can estimate how often large earthquakes strike a fault by studying layers of sediment that past quakes have disturbed. At Corran Marsh, geologist Ama Owusu dug a trench across the Tessel Fault and found evidence of five major earthquakes. Using radiocarbon dating, she determined that the sediment layers in the trench spanned roughly 2,400 years and that the oldest of the quakes struck about 2,100 years ago. The most recent, she concluded, occurred around 340 years ago.
choices: 340 years
480 years
2,100 years
2,400 years
explanation: The text says 'the oldest of the quakes struck about 2,100 years ago.' Choice C matches that number.

A.why: 340 years is the date of the most recent quake, not the oldest. You picked up a number from the next sentence.

B.why: You got 480 by dividing 2,400 years by five quakes. The passage never does this calculation, and the result is not the age of any quake. You reasoned past what the text actually says.

D.why: 2,400 years is how long the sediment layers span. It is the outer limit of the record, not the age of the oldest quake. You confused a range boundary with the specific figure the question asks for.

stem: According to the text, what did Hesse find in the Lindqvist Partbooks?
stimulus: Musicologists have long attributed the Lindqvist Partbooks, an anonymous set of sixteenth-century choral manuscripts, to a single monastery scribe. However, a recent study by musicologist Clara Hesse found three distinct styles of handwriting in the books, along with two different types of paper. Hesse concludes that the partbooks were likely copied by several scribes over a period of years rather than by one person working alone.
choices: Three distinct styles of handwriting
The name of a single monastery scribe
Choral music composed by several scribes
Paper that was all produced in one year
explanation: After 'However,' the text says Hesse 'found three distinct styles of handwriting in the books.' Choice A matches that line.

B.why: The partbooks are anonymous. The single-scribe idea is the older view that Hesse's study challenges, not something she found. You took the view set up before 'However' and treated it as her finding.

C.why: Hesse concludes that several scribes copied the music. She says nothing about who composed it. You changed 'copied' into 'composed,' which is a claim the text never makes.

D.why: Hesse found two different types of paper and concludes that the copying took place 'over a period of years.' You chose the opposite of what she found.

stem: According to the text, which group of users first used the term "glimmy"?
stimulus: Linguists tracing how new words spread have usually relied on newspapers and books. Linguist Mei Tanaka instead examined 1.2 million posts made on a regional online message board between 2008 and 2018. She found that the slang term "glimmy," meaning tired but cheerful, first appeared among users aged 14 to 17. Within about three years, it had spread to users in their twenties. Users over 40, however, rarely adopted the term at all.
choices: Users aged 14 to 17
Users in their twenties
Users over the age of 40
Writers of newspapers
explanation: The text says "glimmy" 'first appeared among users aged 14 to 17.' Choice A matches that line.

B.why: Users in their twenties picked up the term later, after it spread. You chose the second group in the sequence instead of the first.

C.why: The passage says users over 40 'rarely adopted the term at all.' You picked a group the text describes as hardly using the word.

D.why: Newspapers come up only as the sources other linguists usually study. They have nothing to do with who first used "glimmy." You matched a word from the opening sentence without checking what question it answers.
